title: Pentagon claims Ottawa has no plan to meet defence spending target
html:
U.S. Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth listens as President Donald Trump speaks during a news conference at the White House on Friday.Jacquelyn Martin/The Associated Press

The Trump administration is cranking up the pressure on Ottawa to increase defence spending and complete a deal to buy U.S.-made fighter jets by issuing a new “fact sheet” deriding the Canadian military’s lack of operational readiness.

The Pentagon posted the document online Monday, two weeks after U.S. Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth wrote a memo that reportedly puts restrictions on American military personnel attending Canadian conferences and social events.

The missive accuses Canada of having no concrete plan to increase defence spending to 5 per cent of GDP by 2035, as the country agreed to at last year’s NATO summit in The Hague. It also slams Ottawa for taking nearly two decades to reach the previous NATO target of 2 per cent of GDP and highlights the capability shortfalls of Canada’s Army, Navy and Air Force.

“Underinvestment in defense has atrophied the Canadian Armed Forces and limited Canada’s ability to contribute to the defense of North America,” the document says.

It cites the impending retirement of Canada’s fleet of CF-18 fighter jets and Ottawa’s decision last year to review a plan to buy 88 F-35s from Lockheed Martin.

Prime Minister Mark Carney put the brakes on the purchase when U.S. President Donald Trump launched a trade war on Canada, hammering the country with tariffs and threatening to annex it as the “51st state.”

“Ottawa’s prioritization of parochial economic and commercial interests over military optimization introduces further uncertainty for NORAD and will further burden our Joint Force and the American taxpayer,” the Pentagon’s missive says.

The office of Defence Minister David McGuinty did not respond to a request for comment on the fact sheet late Monday.

The document also cites Canada’s lack of airborne early warning and control aircraft and says just one of Canada’s four Victoria-class submarines is seaworthy at any time.

The Washington Post reported Friday that Mr. Hegseth had written the memo the week before last, placing new “restrictions” on the U.S.-Canada defence relationship. But The Globe and Mail reported that neither the Canadian government nor military had been told anything about it.

This past weekend, at the Halifax International Security Forum, Republican Senator Mike Rounds said the memo just required U.S. military personnel to receive approval from their bosses before taking part in events with their Canadian counterparts. He said it did not change anything about actual military co-operation.

“They’re basically limiting some social engagements and they’re asking people to get permission before they come in and do think tanks and so forth,” he said. “We don’t expect any real changes over the way it has been going for the last year or a year and a half.”

The Trump administration had already been blocking officials from attending the Halifax confab since last year.

Earlier this year, the U.S. suspended its participation in the Permanent Joint Board on Defense, an advisory body that it has run with Canada since the Second World War to make recommendations on military planning.

The dispute over military spending has long pitted the U.S. against its NATO allies and has become a central grievance during the Trump administration. In Canada’s case, it has also become bound up with the trade war and bilateral negotiations, which have included discussions of national security as well as commerce.

Canada and other NATO countries signed the 2-per-cent pledge in 2006 and again in 2014. But Ottawa was slow to meet the target. In 2024, then-prime minister Justin Trudeau dismissed it as a “crass mathematical calculation” that wouldn’t “actually make us automatically safer.”

When Mr. Carney took over last year, he boosted funding by more than $80-billion over five years and, this past March, NATO reported that Canada had finally hit the promised spending number. The Prime Minister and every other NATO country but Spain also agreed to Mr. Trump’s new 5-per-cent-by-2035 figure.

So far, however, Mr. Carney’s government has not explained how it will reach that goal, which would entail devoting 3.5 per cent of GDP to core military spending and another 1.5 per cent to security- and defence-related infrastructure.

The 2026 budget released in early November offered few details. It said Canada’s core defence spending will climb to 2.2 per cent this fiscal year, then remain at 2.6 per cent for four years.

The government has played down questions about the imperative to boost defence spending, saying it has plenty of years left before the NATO deadline to increase military expenditure.

With a report from The Associated Press
summary: Missive says Canadian Armed Forces have ‘atrophied’ because of underinvestment
